original_question: Classify all finite projective planes, or at least determine exactly which integers q can occur as their orders. Here a projective plane is a collection of points and lines in which any two lines intersect in exactly one point and any two points lie on exactly one line; when the plane is finite, the number of points is q^2 + q + 1 and each line contains q + 1 points.
target_in_paper: Section 3, unnumbered paragraph on finite projective planes immediately before Theorem 3.3: the open problem of determining the possible orders q of finite projective planes, with the stronger version asking for a classification of such planes, together with the paper's reformulation that a plane of order q exists exactly when a specific vector h(q) is a pure f-vector, hence a pure O-sequence. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the geometric problem the paper highlights: it asks about finite projective planes, uses the two basic incidence axioms, and includes the standard finite-order numerics that a plane of order q has q^2+q+1 points (and lines) and each line contains q+1 points. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))
missing_details: The paper's main paper-specific reformulation is missing: for each q, existence of a finite projective plane of order q is equivalent to the sequence h(q)=(1, q^2+q+1, (q^2+q+1)C(q+1,2), (q^2+q+1)C(q+1,3), ..., (q^2+q+1)C(q+1,q+1)) being a pure f-vector, equivalently a pure O-sequence. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))

To make the algebraic formulation stand alone, one should specify the ambient polynomial ring R=K[y_1,...,y_{q^2+q+1}] over an arbitrary field K, with generators required to be squarefree monomials of degree q+1; this is why the relevant pure O-sequence is actually a pure f-vector. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))

The draft omits the nondegeneracy hypothesis included in the paper's definition of projective plane: there must exist four points no three of which are collinear. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))

For a sharp stand-alone formulation, q should be quantified as an integer q>=2; the paper notes that the Fano plane of order 2 is the smallest projective plane. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))

The paper identifies finite projective planes with Steiner systems S(2,q+1,q^2+q+1), and that identification should be stated if one wants the question to match the surrounding Section 3 discussion. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))

Nearby context in the paper, though not part of the question itself, is that the expected answer is that q should be a prime power, and the authors record the Bruck-Ryser-Chowla necessary condition for q congruent to 1 or 2 mod 4. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))
refined_question: For each integer q>=2, let v=q^2+q+1 and define h(q)=(1, v, vC(q+1,2), vC(q+1,3), ..., vC(q+1,q+1)). Determine exactly for which q the sequence h(q) is a pure O-sequence; equivalently, determine exactly for which q there exists a pure simplicial complex on v vertices with pure f-vector h(q), i.e. a Steiner system S(2,q+1,v), equivalently a finite projective plane of order q. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: Determine exactly which integers q>=2 occur as orders of finite projective planes. Equivalently, decide for which q the sequence h(q) above is a pure f-vector, hence a pure O-sequence. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))
justification: The draft is close to the geometric statement highlighted by the paper, but the paper is a survey on pure O-sequences, and both the introduction and Section 3 frame finite projective planes as an application of pure O-sequence theory. The introduction says that existence of finite projective planes is equivalent to existence of particular pure O-sequences, and the finite-projective-plane paragraph in Section 3 gives the exact iff reformulation using h(q). Because that reformulation addresses existence of a plane of order q, the sharpest paper-faithful stand-alone version is the order/existence problem phrased through h(q), with the geometric projective-plane statement kept as the explicitly equivalent formulation. The nearby Theorem 3.3 supplies context on known necessary conditions, but it is not itself the target problem. ([www3.nd.edu](https://www3.nd.edu/~jmiglior/MNZ5POSexp.pdf))
